div.span: the 6 standardized compilations (by Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawood, Al-Trimidhi, Al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah).

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237)); font-size: 8px;

div.span: Notes: the Quran is claimed to be authored by God (ie. infallible), while the hadith are the works of men (ie. fallible). The Quranic scribes were led by Zaid b. Thabit (writing almost immediately after each revelation), and thousands memorized these revelations (with hundreds who memorized the entire Quran). Abu Bakr (with Zaid b. Thabit) was the first to standardize a full, written copy of the Quran (verified by those who directly witnessed the Quran's revelation), with Hafsah (one of the Prophet's wives) being its guardian. Lastly, Uthman was the one to textually standardize the Quran's accent/diacritics.

font.b: Yes - the Jewish Christians and Gnostics

div.font: - The Jewish Christians believed in Jesus' virgin birth and that he was the Messiah, but rejected Paul as a heretic and practiced Mosaic Law. As we don't have their text, it is also debated whether or not they believed that Jesus was divine.

div.font: Notes: all Jewish Christian writings are lost, and what is known about them only comes from hostile sources, making much of it debated - including whether the "human Jesus" belief was early or later. The Ebionites were a noteworthy sect within the Jewish Christians, only differing by rejecting the virgin birth. After the Bar Kokhba revolt, they (along with the Jews in Rome) were expelled and dispersed throughout Africa, the Mediterranean, and parts of the Arab world. As a result, very little is known about them with a strong certainty, with the only other possible references originating in later 7th-century Arab history.

font.b: No with the Quran, yes with the Hadith (Shia vs. Sunni)

font.span: There are no competing claims for the reliability or content of the Quran.

The closest comparison is the qira'at (diffferent accentual/dialectical recitations) that the Prophet himself is reported to have used, but they are all accepted as authentic and even continue to be openly recited today.

div.span: The only other comparison is the report of the Satanic verses, mentioned by Muslim historians 100–250 years after the Prophet's death. When surah al-Najm was revealed (which ends with the command to prostrate to God) and the Prophet recited it publicly, the Makkan pagans are reported to have prostrated in awe of the Quran, their hearts touched by its power. Out of embarrassment, they later claimed they had heard 1-2 pagan-affirming verses and prostrated for that reason, alleging that Muhammad must have been tricked by Satan without realizing. However, this is a weak biographical report with no supporting transmission, no parallel incident in the historical record, and a motive (pagan embarrassment) that aligns more closely with their behavior outside of this incident. As such, it is not considered a successful challenge to the Quran's reliability or authority.

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(237, 237, 237)); font-size: 8px;

div.span: There was also the Shia/Sunni split, but they differed over the nature of Ali b. Abi Talib, which is who the Shia assert was the rightful caliph after the Prophet's death. They believed that those closest to the Prophet corrupted the religion after he died, fabricating reports in his name to gain political power. As such, they have their own set of hadith compilations, in which the Prophet entrusted the true interpretation of the religion with Ali and his descendants (including Fatima, the Prophet's daughter and Ali's wife).

div.span: unknown oral tradition of Jewish Christians who believed Jesus was a "man of men (ie. naturally born)

div.font: Notes: each chain begins with the earliest preserved source in that transmission. John is the only Gospel writer reported to have witnessed the crucifixion directly, while Paul's letters were written earlier than the Gospels. It is not unusual that the Gospel authors did not identify themselves within the text, since their audiences already knew the authors, with manuscripts being tagged with their names - much like authored books today. The Christian claim is that the Holy Spirit is the primary custodian of truth, ensuring its preservation regardless of historical circumstances.

div.font: Notes: the Islamic claim is that the angel Gabriel - also known as the Holy Spirit and responsible for conveying revelation to all Prophets - is the custodian of the Quran between God and Muhammad. The Quran further asserts that God Himself guarantees its preservation, reinforcing the belief that truth remains distinguishable from falsehood. Additionally, a core difference between Sunni and Shia theology is that Shia Muslims hold the lineage of Ali b. Abi Talib through their imams to be infallible for twelve generations.
